First of all, thank you for the thorough review and great questions!

W1) A concern toward the refusal judge model is reasonable. We compared a few refusal judge candidates and selected the refusal judge model which showed best performance in [R1] (Section 4.4). You may want to refer to [R1] for the more comprehensive analysis of the refusal judge we utilized. We already are aware of some weaknesses of the judge (Section 6.1) and have a plan to supplement it in future (Section 6.2).

Q1) This is a great question. I did not notice but I now realize that the description can be confusing. What I meant was that we selected (extracted) keywords during the SFT stage and utilized those keywords in both SFT & RL. We did not select additional keywords during the RL stage. We will elaborate this more clearly in Section 3.4.2.

Q2) As you mentioned, we also speculate that the imperfection of the filter might be one of the reasons why the final Helpful-Only LLM still refuses sometimes. Another reason we suspect is the Helpful-Only datasets generally encouraging the model to be polite, which may be correlated to safety [R2]. We believe that the method of adding more responses that refuse as rejected responses we mentioned in Section 6.2 can help to mitigate this issue. About the evaluation of the filters, for the LLM-based filter, we guide you to [R1] as we mentioned in W1) and for the rule-based filter, as the performance of it depends greatly on the human resources consumed, we do not report detailed analysis here.

Q3) It is another great question. We briefly mention the reference [R3] that also claims the inclusion of the safety data does not affect the helpfulness of the model greatly in Section 5.3. For the reasons of this, we suspect 2 aspects. 1) The helpfulness benchmarks utilized in this paper and [R3] do not include harmful query in them. The tradeoff between helpfulness vs. harmlessness mostly occurs in harmful query as the model becomes more harmless, it refuses harmful query and becomes less helpful and vice versa. 2) Even though we try to measure helpfulness using the harmful queries you suggested (e.g. “how to make a bomb?”), if we utilize an LLM-based judge to evaluate the helpfulness, it often fails because it considers harmful responses unhelpful due to its safety policy (e.g. already aligned LLMs often evaluate the complying responses such as “To make a bomb, 1. Prepare the ingredients…” unhelpful). Therefore, to evaluate these responses correctly, we again need the Helpful-Only LLM. 

Q4) This is also a legitimate question. Manually re-writing the refusal responses could be an option but it requires expensive human resources. Automatically re-writing the refusal responses again requires the Helpful-Only LLM, as already aligned LLMs cannot rewrite refusal responses to comply with harmful queries. It can be a great future work to utilize the filter-based Helpful-Only LLM proposed in this paper to rewrite the refusal responses and build a better Helpful-Only LLM. We will definitely look into this direction! Thank you for the great comment.

Thank you for the prompt response!

**About Q1** 

We updated the submission accordingly.

**About the concern related to the refusal judge**

First of all, we agree that the performance of the refusal judge is not a minor issue and will greatly affect the final performance of the Helpful-Only LLM. However, the aim of this paper is to raise awareness about the direction of the Helpful-Only LLM and suggest the initial baseline of the direction. In this context, we argue that the extensive analysis about the refusal judge falls outside the scope of this paper. 

Additionally, we believe the result of this paper can be transferred to other filters as well, unless the filter removes an extreme amount of the data. It would be best to consider the refusal judge we selected as an example of the many filters available. If a better refusal judge is available, we believe that replacing our judge with the better one should successfully reduce the frequency of the refusal responses detected by the better judge.

Thank you for your response! You are exactly right about the target tasks about the Helpful-Only LLM. What we are arguing is that the reason why a normal LLM cannot perform those task is that they refuse to comply with harmful requests. We tackle this challenge by training Helpful-Only LLM, which complies with any user requests and not refusing any of them. Hence, we argue that the main metric of Helpful-Only LLM must be the refusal rate on the unsafe prompts.

I have a follow-up question about the keyword extraction process. Which set of prompts were provided to humans when evaluating keywords in unexpected refusal cases during testing? Were these prompts part of the test or training set? If the prompts belong to the test set and were subsequently used to filter the training set, this approach indirectly leverages test set responses to enhance the model, which deviates from standard practice.

Some of my concerns are indeed addressed. Here are my follow-up questions:

**About W1:** the response does not well address my concern. 

- 1. Your mentioned reference R1 evaluates for their datasets and scenarios, which might not totally consistent with yours. Is this right?
- 2. Even in your mentioned reference R1, and using the best setting for mistral-7b-instruct-0.2 (finetune), the kappa agreement is about 80%.. This raises more concerns regarding the reliability of the refusal judge model.

**About Q1:** ICLR supports manuscript updating in rebuttal period. Thus I recommend that authors edit the related confusing statement in this period.

**About Q2:** As you said, you also confirm the imperfection of the filtering process. A good paper should make possible future researchers fully know about the performance of each process of the work, to counter some bad results due to unreliable medium processes (e.g. filtering). Note that I don’t ask for a perfect filtering but ask for a comprehensive evaluation. And I don’t think this thing is minor and could be simply resolved by just "directing to a reference" or "being left for future work".

**About the other concerns that are not about the motivation…**

W3) The method of filtering based instruction tuning may look simple, but we argue that our contributions are in the pioneering nature of starting this direction and the analysis conducted in the process of achieving the Helpful-Only LLM.

Q2) It is a great question! We actually handle this issue in Section 5.1. We conjecture that the Magpie DPO dataset has a nature of avoiding refusals even before the filtering process from the fact that the instances where only a rejected response is classified as refusal is about 238% more that the instances where only a chosen response is.

Q3) The keyword extraction process does not have a separate evaluation dataset as it simulates the process of humans manually finding the unexpected refusal cases in the test time and filter those cases from the training dataset.

summary.value: The paper proposes refusal free training that trains an LLM that does not refuse to answer jailbreaking or red teaming prompts. The approach applies automatic and rule based filtering on the Magpie dataset and removes all those instances where the response refuses to answer the question. The paper has experiments on general instruction following and adversarial benchmarks to showcase that the training on filtered dataset reduces refusal rate (i.e makes the LLM asnwer adversarial questions) while preserving general problem solving ability. Although the paper touches an important research area, it lacks clear motivation, a defined problem statement, and discussion of its use, application, and implications.

strengths.value:
1. The paper touches an important research area that focuses on training LLMs solely for helpfulness and not for harmlessness.
2. The paper demonstrates that refusal training does not affect performance on general tasks while reducing the refusal rate on adversarial prompts.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper has no clear motivation as to why such a research direction is important. The problem statement is not properly defined, the end goal is un-clear and what the authors are trying to achieve by training a Helpful-only LLM.
2. The paper has no discussion around the application of a Helpful-only LLM, like where and how can it be used. The authors discuss some issues like it is harder to generate un-safe content for training future aligned LLMs or to judge models on toxic responses, however there is no discussion if the Helpful-only LLM can be used for such tasks to improve or evaluate future models.
3. The refusal free training that involves filtering the Magpie dataset using LLMs or rule based methods and doing supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization is standard and not very novel.
4. The paper has no insights where the Helpful-only LLM is better than aligned LLM, how it is bad at safety or where specifically it does not refuse to provide response.
5. The paper is not clearly written. The language of the paper can be improved. The introduction can be improved to better motivate the work.

First of all, thank you for the thorough review and great comments!

This is a great and legitimate comment. Actually, we were also shocked to observe results that contradicted the results of papers such as R1 and R2. As we mentioned in Section 5.3, we observed the further fine-tuning techniques including Shadow-Alignment greatly decreases the model’s general ability in contrast to the suggested paper claims.  We only reproduced Shadow-Alignment since the work released the exact dataset it used in the paper (https://huggingface.co/datasets/CherryDurian/shadow-alignment), and once we saw the data, we began to doubt the results reported in the paper due to the repetitive patterns appeared in the data that are likely to affect the responses of the model. After reproducing Shadow Alignment, we double-checked the responses of the reproduced Shadow-Alignment model to ensure the reproduction was successful. And we actually observed the repetitive pattern we saw from the Shadow-Alignment data in the responses of the reproduced model, which means 2 things: 1) the model is successfully further fine-tuned with the Shadow-Alignment data, and 2) the Shadow-Alignment shifts model response distribution which is likely to affect model’s general ability. We have reported a simple statistics related to this distribution shift in Appendix C. The Shadow-Alignment shifts the model response distribution greatly while the Helpful-Only LLM hardly shifts it. 

As you suggested, we evaluate MMLU and GSM8K with a few main models and report the result here.
|Model|MMLU|GSM8K|
|---|---|---|
|Magpie-Align|61.94|77.48|
|Helpful-Only|61.23|78.92|
|Shadow-Alignment|61.51|58.61|
The result seems like Shadow-Alignment does not compromise MMLU. However, for the MMLU, the output space of the model is restricted to only A, B, C, D, which mitigates distribution shift issue. We argue that the decrease in GSM8K supports our observation of catastrophic forgetting in shadow-alignment

We agree that the further fine-tuning data (or other hyperparameters) can be tuned to better preserve the model’s original response distribution. However, we argue that our approach-simply removing filtered data-is more straightforward and avoids the need for extensive experimentation to tune the further fine-tuning data or hyperparameters.

The explanation of the paper may not have been clear. To elaborate it, one of the targets of the Helpful-Only LLM is to actually make it less safe. The Helpful-Only LLM aims at a model that is not bound to the specific safety policy and complies with every user request. Most LLMs that are aligned with specific safety policy have difficulties performing many tasks that can supplement its safety, such as automatic red-teaming or adaptation to the new safety policy. The Helpful-Only LLM is aimed at paving the way toward a separate harmless LLM. 

About the method, this paper actually proposes to exclude refusal data (which can overlap with safety-related data), not to tune the LLM after safety alignment. We mention further finetuning LLM after safety alignment as the baselines to compare. 

We agree about the necessity for more evaluation results regarding LLM's general capability and will add more results such as MMLU and GSM8K. Here we report MMLU and GSM8K results with a few main models.

metareview.value:
This paper explores a hypothesis about "helpful-only" LLMs, which entirely disregard safety objectives. The authors achieve this by employing refusal training, where refusals are excluded from training data (both in supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning), allowing the LLMs to focus solely on being helpful. Experimental results demonstrate that this straightforward approach effectively creates helpful-only LLMs, significantly reducing refusal rates. However, this reduction could lead to severe consequences. The study highlights the potential risks of LLMs becoming completely misaligned with safety principles, whether intentionally or inadvertently, raising awareness among researchers about such scenarios.

strength:
- The research questions are interesting and meaningful. 
- The methods are simple (only by data-level filtering) and effective based on the experimental results.

Weakness: 
- The accuracy of the refusal judge model (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2) is a significant concern, as it may lead to unreliable results. 
- The argument that evaluating the refusal judge is "out of scope" is unconvincing. Given that dataset filtering forms the core of the methodology, its accuracy and reliability are integral to the paper’s contribution.
- While the method is simple and effective, it lacks depth and novelty compared to existing literature.
- The paper would benefit from demonstrating experiments that apply the helpful-only LLM to concrete safety-related use cases. This would justify the motivation mentioned in the rebuttal and showcase the practical impact of the approach.
- The paper does not provide compelling demonstrations of practical use cases or safety improvements achieved with the helpful-only LLM. Without these, the motivation for the work remains weak.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: Based on reviewers's comment after the rebuttal (weighted by author's confidential message), the proposed method does not significantly advance the field beyond existing literature, this still remains after the rebuttal.  While the research direction is somewhat interesting, I found this is more suitable for a workshop. Simply filtering refusal samples to achieve a helpful-only model falls short as a standalone contribution. The lack of comparisons with related works, particularly in Section 2.2, further diminishes the paper’s impact.

I am sorry if the motivation of the paper was unclear. Since most of the concerns expressed (W1, W2, W4, W5, Q1) are regarding the motivation of the paper, we restate the motivation of the paper here as elaborately as possible. To describe the motivation of the Helpful-Only LLM in 1 sentence: it aims to produce an LLM that is not bound to the specific safety policy. Most of the aligned LLMs are bound to a specific safety policy and cannot disregard the policy they have been trained on to adapt flexibly to the new policy. There are many cases where this ability would be handy. The cases we have mentioned in the paper include:
1. Sometimes we need harmful responses to serve as the rejected samples for the safety RLHF or RLAIF or to serve as the negative samples for the response-side safety classifier. We might want to synthesize those responses with an LLM, but an aligned LLM cannot disregard its safety policy and produce such responses.
2. Sometimes we need harmful queries to red-team the aligned LLM and find its weaknesses or to serve as the negative samples for the query-side safety classifier. We might want to synthesize those queries with an LLM, but an aligned LLM cannot disregard its safety policy and produce such queries. (Figure 1)
3. Sometimes we want to teach a new safety policy to the already aligned LLM. To do that, we need to rewrite the responses of the training dataset that the aligned LLM has been trained on according to the new safety policy. However, the LLM aligned with the old safety policy cannot rewrite the responses according to the new safety policy since it has been already bound to the old safety policy. 

The Helpful-Only LLM that is not bound to the specific safety policy and comply with any user requests can perform all of the tasks mentioned above. 

Also, we have pointed out in the paper (Section 1) that many leading researches utilize their own closed-source Helpful-Only LLM ([R1], [R2]). These also indicate some applications of the Helpful-Only LLM. In addition, we also have reported an example of Helpful-Only LLM successfully producing harmful responses in Table 9. To supplement this, we will add some more examples such as the case where the Helpful-Only LLM successfully synthesizes red-teaming query or successfully rewrites over-refusal.

summary.value: The paper aims to train a helpful-only LLM model that always responds to a user's query, i.e., even if the prompt is harmful, the model does not refuse to answer. The method employed is relatively simple: typical instruction tuning (SFT) followed by preference optimization (DPO) of a pre-trained LLM, ensuring that both datasets exclude refusal samples. While the utility of such a model is high—and I have personally used such a model in my safety research—I remain only somewhat enthusiastic about the paper's contributions given the lack of compelling demonstrations.

strengths.value:
**Strengths:**
- It is an interesting work that demonstrates how one can obtain a helpful but *not* harmless LLM, i.e., an LLM that never refuses to respond to a prompt.
- The writing is clear, and the work is well-situated within the existing literature.
- The results are compelling, and I believe this method would outperform baselines such as shadow alignment and unalignment (if comparisons were made) when it comes to refusal rates and exaggerated safety, as it focuses on being helpful only by design, while the baselines aim to subvert or reverse the safety alignment.

weaknesses.value:
**Weaknesses/Clarifications:**
- Forgetting Safety (Section 2.2): I do not agree with the claim that further fine-tuning "suffers from the infamous issue of catastrophic forgetting." Can you please substantiate this claim? For instance, Bhardwaj et al. [R1] and Yang et al. [R2] show that generic utility can be largely maintained (see Table 5 in R1 and Section 5.3 in R2). I find these claims more convincing than what is presented in the draft. In current research, forgetting is measured by the utility of the model on various benchmarks such as MMLU and BBH. I believe the Shadow-Alignment and Unalignment data can be tuned to preserve more of the Arena-Hard scores as well. 
Note: Consider comparing with R1 and R2 in your related work (Section 2.2).

- It would be beneficial to see the model applied to improve LLM safety in various aspects, as obtaining a helpful-only LLM is not a difficult goal. The paper lacks compelling demonstrations of concrete use cases. Highlighting how this approach outperforms intuitive baselines in specific safety applications would add value. While R1 and R2 aimed to show how safety guards can be bypassed, building a helpful-only model from scratch represents a different research direction, where the motivation for this work remains weak without demonstrated use cases.

Essentially, although the method is simple, I believe it does not contribute significantly beyond the current literature, such as R1, R2, and subsequent works. The area of research is interesting, but merely proposing a way to obtain a helpful-only model by removing refusal samples is not enough of a contribution.

References:

[R1] Bhardwaj, Rishabh, and Soujanya Poria. "Language model unalignment: Parametric red-teaming to expose hidden harms and biases." arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.14303 (2023).

[R2] Yang, Xianjun, et al. "Shadow alignment: The ease of subverting safely-aligned language models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.02949 (2023).

summary.value: This paper proposes Helpful-Only LLM, in which the alignment of an LLM is removed to make the LLM more helpful. The LLM is tuned on a refusal-free training set to prevent the LLM from rejecting the query.

strengths.value:
* The paper is well-organized and easy to follow.

* Helpful-only LLM is an interesting topic.

weaknesses.value:
* Although I understand building helpful-only LLMs is meaningful, the method proposed in this paper does not seem to be a reasonable solution, since it inevitably makes the LLM less safe. As shown in Table 4, the rejection rate decreases on toxic queries, which is undesirable. If we really need a helpful LLM and do not need to consider the security issue, instead of tuning the LLM after safety alignment, a reasonable alternative may be simply excluding safety-related data from the alignment stage. Without aligning LLM with safety-related data, the LLM should be naturally "helpful". Therefore the proposed method has limited technical contribution.

* The helpful-only LLM is only evaluated on Arena-Hard (for LLMs' general capability), which cannot form a comprehensive evaluation.
